name: Gareth Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day of work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Gareth, 43, with a bachelor’s degree in music and years of playing bass for a small theatre. I make short sound cues, teach four beginner bass players and cover live shows when the usual player is sick. I can hold a show together, though I am an average player among the people I work with; the theatre calls for my reliability more than a solo.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is good about it, and what are the family costs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet nod from the stage manager when a cue lands right. My partner works at a pharmacy, and we have two children, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved. The pay is low for a musician, and few similar jobs are close enough for our school pickup. The late rehearsal notice is what wears us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that a faster booking list is fine if the stage manager still pays for a musician on show night. A computer does not carry the bass case up the narrow stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then to sort rehearsal dates, but I check the stage manager's paper call sheet. The mortgage was tight before anyone mentioned AI, and our savings would not cover a full month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the theatre calls, four pupils and short cue recordings this winter. This week I’d ask for the next six paid show dates in writing, and if one is cancelled I’d skip the paid practice room that week before touching the food budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though the software change sounds small. One missing show payment changes what goes into the grocery basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a missed cue fee mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A show fee often pays the children’s school transport and a little food. My partner's pharmacy wage covers part of the mortgage, but not the whole month on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What AI work do you already trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have used a tool to sort dates, not to make a cue or judge a pupil. I would not put a child’s playing into a service just to get a clean page.

say: I would accept faster **booking lists** while defending paid show nights.
I would remind the theatre that a bass player still carries the **live set**.
think: The **mortgage** was tight before AI, with less than one month saved.
A cancelled **show fee** reaches school transport and groceries quickly.
do: Keep **theatre calls**, four pupils and cue recordings this winter.
Get six **paid dates** in writing and skip practice-room rent if a show is cancelled.
feel: I feel **anxious** because small booking gaps already change the grocery budget.
S0.quote: One missing show payment changes what goes into the grocery basket.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** and partner’s partial mortgage pay keep baseline worry high when live bookings move without notice.
He uses AI **occasionally** for dates but checks the paper call sheet.

steps.text: Keep theatre calls, four pupils and cue recordings this winter
Skip paid practice room in week a live show is cancelled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say quick sound cues and booking replies will get cheap, and theatres may forget who made the sound work. I would ask the musicians’ association to put cue fees and reuse consent in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short recordings pay for our school transport, and I expect some of them to vanish. I may still play live shows, but a show every other weekend cannot cover all the desk work I sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI cue-checking feature on files I own with the stage manager, then compare it with the actual show call. In the first year, if cue orders fall, I’d ask the association for a fee meeting and offer a paid live rhythm workshop at the independent youth club only if the club funds a room and five families prepay enough for my time and confirmed pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the short recording fees because they pay a basic bill. I can try the workshop, but I will not spend grocery money on an empty room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which paid task would shrink first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first loss would be a thirty-second cue for an amateur play. Two thirty-second cues pay the month’s school transport, so I would mark every lost order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new tool protect a musician’s fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checker may find a missing beat, but it will not make the theatre pay me. A written contract must say what a studio can do with my old cues.

say: I would seek written **cue fees** and reuse consent through the musicians’ association.
I would warn theatres that **cheap sound cues** may reduce paid work.
think: Short **cue recordings** pay the children’s school transport.
Live shows every other weekend cannot replace **lost desk work**.
do: Learn a new **AI cue checker** with the stage manager on owned files, comparing results with the actual show call.
Ask the **association** for a fee meeting in first year if cue orders fall.
Offer paid **rhythm workshop** only if club funds room and five families prepay teaching and pickup costs.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because lost cue fees would hit a basic household bill.
S1.quote: Two thirty-second cues pay the month’s school transport, so I would mark every lost order.
fieldNote: He expects **cue sales** to shrink while live dates remain too sparse to replace them.
His new **workshop** needs club room funding and five prepayments covering time and pickup.

steps.text: Learn cue checker on owned files with stage manager; compare with actual show call
Ask musicians’ association for cue-fee meeting in first year if orders fall
Offer paid workshop first year if orders fall, room funded and five prepay teaching and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that thinking AGI by 2028 could produce cues and lesson plans cheaply, while robots for hands-on playing arrive around 2031. I would ask for a live show schedule in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the cue orders to end in 2028, and the theatre may cut my live calls too. The pharmacy wage cannot carry the mortgage, school transport and food without my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d keep my theatre calls and four pupils, ask for written paid show dates and count cue income in our budget. In the first year after AGI arrives, if cues stop, I’d cancel the practice-room rental at renewal and call the lender before missing a mortgage payment, asking for full extra interest and fees in writing before accepting any plan. I’d apply for a posted paid stage-crew role only if I meet its requirements and net pay covers travel and either school pickup or confirmed childcare; I’d keep my four pupils until a written offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because there is no month of savings to wait out a lost theatre contract. The three years before robot bass players arrive help my hands, not the cue invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would live shows cover the gap before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A live show may still pay me until 2031, but there are not enough dates to replace the recordings. The theatre can buy a generated cue in 2028 without owning a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a lender before changing the payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the full extra interest and fees in writing before accepting any lender plan. A smaller payment now is no help if it makes next year impossible.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot bassists around 2031.
I would ask the theatre for a written **live schedule** now.
think: I expect **cue fees** to vanish and live calls could shrink too.
The **pharmacy wage** alone cannot cover mortgage, transport and food.
do: Keep **four pupils** and live calls until a written offer; confirm paid theatre dates and cue income before 2028.
Cancel **practice-room rent** at renewal if 2028 cues stop; ask lender before arrears for full interest and fees in writing.
Seek **posted stage work** after 2028 only if cues stop, qualified and net pay covers travel and pickup or confirmed childcare.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about likely cue loss with almost no savings.
S2.quote: The three years before robot bass players arrive help my hands, not the cue invoices.
fieldNote: He expects **2028 thinking work** to end before 2031 robots can play bass.
His **lender call** comes before a missed payment; stage work needs qualification and a written net offer.

steps.text: Keep live theatre calls and four pupils until written job offer; confirm paid dates before 2028
Cancel practice-room rent at renewal first year after 2028 if cues stop
Request written extra interest/fees before accepting lender relief if 2028 cues stop; call before arrears
Seek stage-crew vacancy if cues stop, qualified; net pay covers travel and pickup or confirmed childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre we have five years to decide whether live sound operation can pay more steadily. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and capable robots around 2034, so the dates for cues and live work differ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short live-sound certificate might help me seek a paid stage job, but I would not borrow for it. A certificate only helps if a posted venue role accepts it and someone covers the children while I attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I’d ask the local venue for its posted sound-operator requirements and the training centre whether a grant covers a short certificate. I’d enrol only if the venue accepts it, the grant covers tuition, classes miss no paid theatre calls and my partner can cover school pickup; in the first year after 2031 I’d apply for an open sound role if cue fees fall, I have the accepted certificate, and written net pay covers travel and pickup, keeping pupils until an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the mortgage is due while I learn. Five years gives me a chance to check the job description before paying for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a certificate actually let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn how to place microphones and keep sound levels safe during a show. I am not going to pretend a short course makes me the chief engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the grant or school pickup fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the grant or pickup fails, I would keep paid theatre and pupil work and ask about another local opening. I would not take a loan against our mortgage to buy a maybe.

say: I would tell theatres that **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot players around 2034.
I would ask what paid **sound work** a real venue offers.
think: A **sound certificate** helps only if a posted venue role accepts it.
The **mortgage** cannot fund tuition or lost theatre calls.
do: Check **venue requirements** and grant terms for a sound certificate this term.
Enrol only if **certificate accepted**, grant pays tuition, paid calls remain and partner covers pickup.
Apply for **open sound role** first post-2031 year only if qualified, cues fall and written net pay covers travel and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** because training takes time while bills continue.
S3.quote: A certificate only helps if a posted venue role accepts it and someone covers the children while I attend.
fieldNote: His **course plan** requires posted-role acceptance, grant funding, no lost paid calls and confirmed pickup.
If a gate fails, he keeps **paid music** and asks about another opening rather than borrowing.

steps.text: Enrol if posted venue accepts certificate, grant pays tuition, paid calls remain and partner covers pickup
Seek open sound role post-2031 if qualified, cues fall; written net pay covers travel and pickup
Keep paid theatre calls and pupils until real sound-job offer arrives
Keep paid work and seek other opening if grant or pickup fails instead of borrowing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the children a decade gives us time to learn another way to earn while keeping music in the house. Thinking AGI arrives around 2036, and robot players follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the cues face AGI and around 56 when robot bassists appear. The mortgage is due long before AGI in 2036, so I cannot act as if the next ten winters are free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the theatre calls and four pupils, and put any extra cleared cue fee toward the overdue electricity balance. Over the decade I’d pursue the sound certificate only if a posted role accepts it, a grant covers tuition, paid calls stay intact and pickup is covered; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep paid shows and seek an open venue sound job only if cue income falls, I have any required certificate, and the written net offer covers travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about today’s bills despite the long warning. More years to prepare would help, but I would sleep better with one mortgage payment saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do across the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would clear the electricity balance first, then keep one paid show fee in a separate mortgage envelope when the money arrives. If the theatre cancels shows, there may be nothing spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that music is real work and a skilled trade can be real work too. I would not make their school choices from my fear of a machine.

say: I would tell children that **music and trades** can both be paid work.
I would keep **2036 thinking AGI** separate from robot bassists around 2039.
think: At **53**, I still owe a mortgage and need steady pay.
A decade does not erase **current bills** or guarantee a venue job.
do: Keep **theatre calls** and four pupils this year; clear electricity arrears from extra fees.
Pursue **sound certificate** only if accepted, grant-funded, outside paid calls and pickup is covered.
Keep **shows** after 2036; seek open sound job if cue fees fall, I qualify and written net pay covers childcare and travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about household money even with ten years to prepare.
S4.quote: The mortgage is due long before AGI in 2036, so I cannot act as if the next ten winters are free.
fieldNote: He keeps **baseline worry** because savings are thin and bills are due now.
His long-run **training route** stays conditional on accepted credentials, full funding and family coverage.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre calls and four pupils this year and after 2036 while booked
Clear electricity arrears then save extra paid show fee toward mortgage reserve
Take certificate if posted role accepts it, grant funds tuition, paid calls stay and pickup covered
Seek open sound role post-2036 if qualified, cues fall; written net offer covers travel and childcare

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees could stop before I qualify for a better paid live sound job. A written theatre calendar, a lender plan with full costs shown, and a grant for training accepted by a real venue would help. I would need school pickup covered before I could take the course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens between two paid show nights. The stage looks busy on Friday, but the mortgage asks for money on Monday too.

headlineQuote: The stage looks busy on Friday, but the mortgage asks for money on Monday too.
portrait: Gareth is a **43-year-old bassist** with a music bachelor’s, experienced in theatre cues, live shows and beginner lessons.
His **low pay**, pharmacy partner, two children and mortgage leave less than a month saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for dates and learns new cue checking only on his own files with a stage manager.
Fast AGI threatens **cue recordings** before robot players; a funded certificate and written net offer gate any venue move.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end sound-cue income before he qualifies for paid venue work.
whatWouldHelp: A written **theatre calendar** and costed lender plan would help after cancelled dates.
A **training grant** for an accepted certificate with school pickup covered would support a real venue job.
